st-catherines.summaryNote: St. Catherines enter this game as the only undefeated team in the league, having run through a gauntlet that includes a dramatic 22-21 takedown of Hoover — a team that had been considered among the league's elite. They score nearly 19 runs per game and hit as a collective monster, with no clear weak spot in a rotation that has sent as many as 17 different players to the plate across five weeks. Their depth is their defining edge: even role players carry dangerous averages, and the lineup rarely gives pitchers a breather from top to bottom.
st-catherines.lineupNote: The Tigers rotate a deep 17-player roster, with several contributors appearing in only 1-2 games yet posting elite averages; expect fresh threats in every inning and no true bottom of the order.

lineup.tip: Malaspina is the hottest bat on a scorching roster — 13-for-14 on the season with a perfect 11-for-11 over his last three games, including a home run. He leads the team in runs (+5 R vs. RBI differential) and scored 12 times in just 4 games, suggesting he reaches base and creates chaos every trip. ISO of .286 signals real extra-base pop beyond the gaudy contact rate.
lineup.pitchTip: Attack early in the count with low-and-away off-speed to avoid putting him on base; avoid anything elevated — he turns on heat consistently. Do not fall behind 1-0.

lineup.tip: Besse is the most dangerous extra-base threat on the team by a wide margin — an ISO of .818 is extraordinary, driven by 1 HR, 2 triples, and 2 doubles in only 11 at-bats across 3 games. He drives in 1.33 runs per hit (12 RBI on 9 hits) and went 9-for-11 in his last three outings. Every hit he squares up has the potential to clear the bases.
lineup.pitchTip: Pitch him outside and down; he punishes middle-in deliveries to the gaps and over the fence. If runners are on with fewer than two outs, consider pitching around him — his RBI rate is unmatched on this roster.

lineup.tip: Zlatunich mirrors Besse in destruction: ISO .857, a HR, a triple, and 8 RBI on 6 hits in just 2 games — tied for the highest RBI/H ratio on the team at 1.33. He went 6-for-7 in his last three games, and his -3 R differential confirms he is a true run-driver rather than a table-setter. With only 7 ABs, his numbers are small-sample but alarming.
lineup.pitchTip: Limited track record makes him somewhat unpredictable, but the extra-base power is real. Keep the ball down and off the plate; do not leave anything belt-high — he will turn it into extra bases.

lineup.pitchTip: Work him up and in to reduce his gap power; he is most dangerous on middle-away pitches that he can drive to right-center. Do not pitch around him carelessly — the runner situation will typically make him worth attacking carefully.

gamePlan.heading: Pitch around Besse and Zlatunich with runners on base.
gamePlan.tip: These two players share the team's highest RBI/H ratio at 1.33 and carry ISO values of .818 and .857 respectively — combined they have 20 RBI in just 5 combined games. If a base is open in a run-scoring situation, take it rather than challenge either bat.

gamePlan.heading: Play deep outfield and shift toward the gaps.

gamePlan.heading: Keep the ball low to neutralize the team's .899 slugging percentage.
gamePlan.tip: The Tigers slug .899 as a team — elite by any measure. Elevated pitches (waist-high and above) are routinely turned into extra-base hits. Ground balls and low contact limit the SLG; an infield that stays sharp on hard grounders is the best path to keeping this offense under 19 runs.

The 22-21 win over Hoover showed this team can survive bad innings and manufacture runs from anywhere in a 17-player rotation. Maintain focus and pitch intensity through the bottom of the order — there is no rest here.

lincoln-lions.summaryNote: The Lincoln Lions are a disciplined, contact-heavy lineup that punished a weak Franklin squad 20-11 but have struggled against elite competition, getting outscored 32-8 in blowout losses to St. Catherines and Hoover. At 3-2-1 they remain a legitimate mid-tier threat: they spread hits across the full lineup, post a .471 team average, and rarely go cold as a unit. Their Achilles heel is a lack of true power — just one HR and a modest .596 team SLG — meaning they depend on stringing together contact and manufacturing runs.

His ISO of .200 is modest but his sheer contact rate and RBI/H of 0.75 make him a constant threat with runners on.

His 5-for-8 recent form shows no cooling off, and he did his damage across all six games including the Franklin blowout.
lineup.pitchTip: He has HR power — do not leave anything elevated or middle-out. Jam him inside early and avoid the outer third. If he falls behind in the count, pitch him up and off the plate to chase.

lineup.pitchTip: Respect his extra-base power — keep the ball down and do not elevate. With his high RBI/H ratio he is at his most dangerous with runners on; consider pitching around him in those spots if first base is open.

lineup.tip: Moorthy leads the team with 5 doubles, pairing a .588 AVG with a .294 ISO and 7 RBI. His -4 R differential hints that he bats lower in the order or hits into outs with runners ahead, but his gap-to-gap doubles production is real. He went 5-for-7 over his last three games, showing consistent contact with power to the gaps.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a gap hitter who drives the ball to the alleys — shade your outfield toward the gaps. Keep pitches off the outside corner to limit his ability to extend through the zone.

lineup.tip: Katz is the Lions' best table-setter: 9 hits in 20 AB, 2 triples, a +4 R differential (6 R, 2 RBI), and consistent presence at the top of the lineup. His speed on the basepaths makes those triples legitimate scoring threats. Despite a 5-for-10 recent stretch he remains reliable.
lineup.pitchTip: He has speed — if he reaches base, be aware of the running game immediately. His low ISO (.200) means he is not a power threat; challenge him with inside fastballs and limit soft stuff away that he can poke into the gap.

He has very little power (ISO .071, 1 double) but has become a reliable contact hitter who gets on base. His recent form suggests he has figured something out at the plate.

His -2 R differential suggests he hits in the middle of the order and drives in others rather than scoring himself. He went 3-for-8 recently, which is solid production.
lineup.pitchTip: He is dangerous with runners on given his RBI/H rate — consider intentional or careful pitching with runners in scoring position. Elevate pitches to induce pop-ups rather than gap shots.

lineup.tip: Reynolds has the highest RBI/H ratio on the team at 1.25 — he drives in more runners than he collects hits, which means he consistently hits with runners on base. Only 4 hits in 11 AB but 5 RBI, pointing to timely clutch hitting. His 3-for-8 recent form and -3 R differential confirm he is an RBI-first, middle-order bat.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a clutch situational hitter — with runners on, do not miss your spot. Pitch him up and away to limit hard contact; he likely sits on middle pitches to drive in runs, so work the periphery of the zone.

lineup.tip: Kloster is a steady presence across all six games with a .412 average and low strikeout profile implied by his .059 ISO — he puts the ball in play almost every at-bat. His +2 R differential and 4 runs scored show he gets on base and creates chances for the lineup behind him.
lineup.pitchTip: Low power, high contact — challenge him in the zone and trust your defense. He is likely to put the first good pitch in play, so set up your fielders before the pitch rather than trying to overpower him.

lineup.tip: Csongradi has appeared in only 4 games but has been productive: .417 AVG, 4 runs scored, and a 4-for-9 recent stretch suggesting he has hit the ground running when available. His +2 R differential means he scores when he gets on base, making him a useful table-setter when he is in the lineup.
lineup.pitchTip: Limited sample size but steady contact — treat him as a solid mid-lineup bat and do not groove pitches. Work him with off-speed to create weak contact given his lack of ISO power.

lineup.tip: Ou has a reasonable .462 season average but cooled significantly over his last three games (2-for-8, .250). His -2 R differential and only 1 run scored all season suggest he bats deep in the order and does not reach base as often as his AVG implies — possibly poor plate appearances in key spots.
lineup.pitchTip: He is in a slump — attack him early in the count with fastballs in the zone. His recent cold stretch (2-for-8) suggests he may be chasing; exploit that with a breaking ball off the plate after an early strike.

lineup.tip: Kim is a solid contact bat with .385 AVG, 2 doubles, and 5 hits in 13 AB across 5 games. His 3-for-8 recent form is about average for his season pace, and his even R differential (+0) places him in a neutral lineup spot. He does not profile as a power or table-setting threat but is not an easy out.
lineup.pitchTip: No significant power or speed threat — pitch him in the zone and make him earn it. Mix in off-speed on the outer edge; his 2 doubles suggest he can use the whole field, so do not pitch exclusively one way.

players.tip: Martinez is the only Lion with a HR and the only one with an ISO above .300. His .389 ISO across 18 AB is genuinely elite for this league and he has shown power in multiple games. In the Franklin 20-11 blowout he was part of a barrage; he has also contributed in tight wins over Burlingame and Roosevelt Blue.

Moorthy's ISO of .294 is borderline elite for this lineup, driven by a team-leading 5 doubles. He is a gap hitter rather than a pull power threat but the doubles volume is a real concern — one extra runner on base turns many of those into RBI opportunities.

Lau complements his RBI production with gap power — three doubles and a triple means he hits the ball to the outfield with authority. His triple in particular suggests he can leg out extra-base hits on balls in the gap that slower runners would hold to doubles.

Lau has one triple alongside his power numbers, showing he can leg it out when he gets to the gaps. His combination of contact and speed makes him dangerous on any ball that falls in the outfield.

Zeman has only 4 games played but posted a .400 average with a 4-for-7 recent stretch. With limited AB he is somewhat unknown and could be finding his footing — do not give him a free pass. He has zero doubles, so he is purely a contact hitter to watch.

Reynolds is easy to overlook with a .364 average, but his 1.25 RBI/H ratio is the best on the team by a wide margin — he hits with runners on and delivers. Only 4 games played means he may not get flagged in routine scouting, making him a true surprise threat in big moments.

sections.title: Table Setters (score more than they drive in)

players.tip: Martinez is both a table-setter and a run-producer — his +4 R differential (10 R, 6 RBI) shows he gets on base and scores frequently, while his 1 HR and .389 ISO mean he is also a real power threat. He is likely batting near the top of the order due to his combination of getting on base and driving runners in.

Katz is a pure table-setter: 6 runs scored versus only 2 RBI (+4 differential), with 2 triples and consistent contact at .450 AVG. He reaches base, uses his speed, and scores — the Lions likely bat him at or near the top. Against us, shutting down Katz before he gets to scoring position is critical.

Kloster is a contact-first table-setter who scores twice as often as he drives in runs. His .412 average and near-zero strikeout profile (implied by .059 ISO) mean he gets on base and relies on the lineup behind him to bring him home. Prevent him from reaching in the first place.

Csongradi has a +2 R differential in only 4 games, suggesting he gets on base and scores at a solid clip relative to his limited appearances. His .417 average means he is not a free out even though he lacks ISO pop.

gamePlan.heading: Shade outfield toward the alleys for Moorthy and Lau.
gamePlan.tip: Moorthy leads the team with 5 doubles and Lau has added 3 more — the Lions drive the ball into the gaps repeatedly. Position your left and right fielders toward the alleys and be prepared to cut off balls early rather than allowing them to roll to the wall for extra-base hits.

gamePlan.heading: Neutralize Benveniste early and protect against his RBI production.
gamePlan.tip: Benveniste is batting .800 with 9 RBI and has been 8-for-9 over his last three games — he is locked in and dangerous. He should not see a hittable pitch with runners in scoring position. With first base open and runners on, consider pitching around him; his RBI/H of 0.75 means stranding him is better than giving him a chance to drive in two.

gamePlan.heading: Attack French and Kloster early — do not let streaks extend.
gamePlan.tip: French is on a 6-for-7 tear and Kloster is a steady .412 contact bat; both have minimal power (ISO .071 and .059) but reach base reliably. Challenge them in the zone with first-pitch strikes, keep the ball down, and trust your defense. Allowing them to reach creates pressure on the next three or four batters who are genuine run producers.

gamePlan.heading: Be strategic pitching to Reynolds and Gilmore with runners on base.
gamePlan.tip: Reynolds has a 1.25 RBI/H ratio and Gilmore 0.83 — these two are the Lions' most clutch situational hitters. Both show significant negative R differentials (-3 and -2 respectively), confirming they bat with runners already on and deliver. With any runner on second or third, elevate pitches to induce pop-ups rather than giving them anything to drive into the outfield.

gamePlan.heading: Exploit the Lions' lack of elite power — do not be afraid to attack the zone.
gamePlan.tip: Lincoln has only 1 HR and a .596 team SLG (compare to Hoover's .873). Martinez is the lone power threat; the rest of the lineup is contact-and-gap. You can attack the zone against most of the lineup without fear of a home run rally. The Lions scored only 3 runs against us in week 5 (3-14 loss) — their offense collapses when you force them into contact situations on good pitches rather than walking them into counts.

washington-wildkittens.summaryNote: The Washington Wildkittens are a dangerous .500 club whose 3-3 record dramatically undersells their offensive firepower — three of their losses came by a single run, including a gut-punch 21-22 defeat to Franklin and a 14-15 heartbreaker against Hoover. Geheran leads the charge with a team-best 17 hits and 15 RBI across six games, anchoring a balanced lineup that scores 13+ runs per game. Despite carrying zero home runs, the Wildkittens punish gaps with 14 doubles and generate runs in volume through a relentless contact attack and clutch RBI production from multiple bats.
washington-wildkittens.lineupNote: Washington rotates 13+ players with near-universal depth — ten players have logged three or more games, and the bottom third of the order can still hurt you with run-scoring contact. Expect regular rotation at all spots; no clear weak link in the batting order.

lineup.tip: Geheran is the team's offensive engine — 17 hits and 15 RBI in 6 games, an 0.88 RBI/H ratio that makes him the most dangerous contact RBI producer on the roster. His ISO of .217 (3 doubles, 1 triple) means he extends at-bats for extra bases. He was a factor in the close week4 win over McKinley-2 (15-14) and the week5 near-miss vs Franklin. Recent form is 9-for-12 over last 3 games — he is not cooling down.
lineup.pitchTip: Work him away and low; he drives inside pitches with authority to produce RBI. Change speeds, avoid the heart of the zone, and do not leave anything elevated middle-in — that is his extra-base territory.

lineup.tip: Adams has the highest RBI/H on the team at a perfect 1.00 — every hit he gets scores a run. In only 3 games (10 AB) he has produced 7 RBI to go alongside 4 runs scored, with a triple on top. His .700 AVG and .200 ISO are elite for a part-time role, and his 7-for-10 recent stretch means he may be earning more starts. A legitimate middle-of-order threat whenever he is in.
lineup.pitchTip: He hits with runners on base — do not let him see fastballs in the strike zone with men on. Pitch to generate weak contact; avoid leaving anything in his pull zone with runners aboard.

lineup.tip: Roth has the highest ISO on the team at .375 despite zero home runs — he generates that extra-base value entirely through 2 doubles and a team-high 2 triples in just 4 games. His plus-5 R_diff makes him a genuine run-scorer, and his 6-for-12 recent form shows he is active. He is the premier triples threat on this roster — a ball hit in the gap has a real chance of going to third.
lineup.pitchTip: Keep the ball out of the gaps at all costs. Pitch him inside to jam contact; an outfield playing at normal depth gives him room to stretch singles into triples. OF should shade in slightly and favor the alleys when Roth bats.

lineup.tip: Poucher has reached base 15 times in 23 at-bats (.652) and is as consistent a table-setter as the Wildkittens have. His R_diff of +3 confirms he scores more than he drives in, and his 9-for-11 over the last 3 games is the best recent form on the team by at-bat efficiency. Low ISO (.087) means he is a singles machine — he will clog the bases and force your defense to play clean.
lineup.pitchTip: He makes contact at an elite rate; do not walk him, as that puts runners on cheaply. Pitch aggressively in the zone early, use the corners to generate ground balls, and get him out quickly before he can put a hit together with runners on.

lineup.tip: Saifher leads the team in at-bats (26) and has 11 RBI across 6 games — his 0.73 RBI/H marks him as a consistent run producer in the middle of the order. He contributes both a double and a triple for extra-base range and his 8-for-13 recent stretch shows sustained production. He was part of the close game vs McKinley-2 and the Franklin battle — he produces when it counts.
lineup.pitchTip: He sees a lot of at-bats, which means he is patient and selective. Do not give him anything fat in run-scoring situations. Work the outer half and break away from him to generate pop-outs rather than line drives.

lineup.tip: Miles is a well-rounded threat in 4 games — .571 AVG, 3 doubles, ISO of .214, and a nearly neutral R_diff (+1) that shows he both scores and drives in. His 6-for-10 recent form keeps him in the meat of the order. Three doubles in 14 at-bats is a rate that demands gap coverage from the outfield whenever he is up.
lineup.pitchTip: He pulls the ball for extra bases — shade the corners and pitch him away to deny the pull-side gap. Soft contact away and down is the target; avoid anything left middle-away at thigh height.

lineup.tip: Matsurra is a pure table-setter — .562 AVG, +4 R_diff (8 R vs 4 RBI), and an 8-for-10 stretch over the last 3 games that is the hottest recent window on the team. Zero ISO (.000) means he lives and dies by singles, but his ability to reach base and score puts constant pressure on the defense. He scores in bulk when the lineup behind him is clicking.
lineup.pitchTip: Challenge him early in the count — he is a contact hitter who does not pull for extra bases. Get him out quickly to prevent him from becoming a baserunner for the power bats behind him.

lineup.tip: Sando has a quiet profile — no extra-base hits, zero ISO — but his 0.78 RBI/H is above the key 0.7 threshold, making him an efficient run driver via singles with runners on base. His 6-for-10 recent form shows consistency over 5 games. He will not beat you in the gap, but he will hurt you with runners in scoring position.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a situational singles hitter — pitch him in ways that strand runners rather than letting him hit soft singles up the middle. Infield corners should expect routine grounders; stay home on the bases to avoid getting burned by his contact ability.

lineup.tip: Mello matches Adams for the best RBI/H ratio on the team at exactly 1.00 — 7 hits for 7 RBI. His lower AVG (.467) means he can be retired, but any contact tends to drive runs. Two doubles add extra-base value in 15 at-bats. He has been active over 4 games and contributed to several high-scoring innings in the Franklin and McKinley-2 games.
lineup.pitchTip: Treat him like Adams — do not let him see hittable pitches with runners on base. His RBI rate is elite; pitch around him in run-scoring situations if the lineup situation allows it.

Zero ISO suggests pure contact hitting with no extra-base ceiling, but his on-base ability makes him a scoring threat. He is a recent addition to the lineup and should be taken seriously given his .545 clip.
lineup.pitchTip: Get him out early — his value is entirely contact-based. Soft toss to the corners limits his ability to drive the ball; do not let him work deep counts where his contact skills favor him.

lineup.tip: Sandell provides solid depth production in 3 games — .462 AVG, 2 doubles, and a +1 R_diff showing balanced contribution. His ISO of .154 is decent and he has been consistent at 6-for-13 over his last 3 games. He fills in ably and adds to the team's depth threat in the bottom third of the order.
lineup.pitchTip: He is an extra-base type via doubles — keep the ball down and in to prevent line drives to the gaps. He is manageable but not an easy out; avoid complacency late in the lineup.

His .316 AVG is the lowest in the lineup but his run-scoring impact is outsized. However, his 2-for-9 recent stretch suggests a cold stretch; he may be slotted lower or sitting soon.
lineup.pitchTip: He is currently the weakest bat in recent form — attack him aggressively in the zone. His value is reaching base, not hitting for power; get him out quickly and do not walk him into a scoring position for the bats behind him.

He is the closest thing Washington has to a pure power threat and his gap-to-triple speed makes him the most dangerous hitter when the outfield plays deep.

Geheran combines the highest hit total (17) with a strong ISO of .217 — 3 doubles and a triple give him extra-base production alongside his elite RBI total. He is the team's all-around best player and would be the anchor of any power section despite the team carrying no home runs.
Miles has ISO .214 driven by three doubles in 14 at-bats — a doubles rate that is among the best on the team. He is a gap hitter in the truest sense and should be defended accordingly.
Three doubles in 14 at-bats — Miles is the most reliable gap hitter in the lineup. Outfield must stay honest in the alleys when he bats.
Geheran and Miles share the team double lead (3 each). His extra-base rate across 23 at-bats is consistent and repeatable.
Saifher adds doubles and a triple from high in the order. Outfield must play honest depth against him in the alleys.
Sandell adds two doubles in only 13 at-bats — a strong rate for a depth player. Do not play him shallow.

Roth is the #1 triples threat on the team with 2 triples in just 16 at-bats. His speed in the gaps is genuine. OF must play conservative depth and cut off balls in the alleys before they roll to the wall.
Geheran added a triple among his 17 hits. At .739 AVG he reaches base so often that any miscue in the outfield extends into an extra base.
Saifher's triple adds to the triples threat pool. At .577 AVG over 26 AB he is a reliable contact hitter who can stretch a hit.

The team's top RBI producer by volume and rate. In the week4 15-14 win over McKinley-2 and the week5 21-22 loss to Franklin he was the engine of the offense. 15 RBI in 6 games is exceptional without a home run.
Perfect RBI/H in 3 games — Adams converts contact to runs at the highest rate on the team. Small sample but completely clean ratio.

gamePlan.heading: Play the outfield at moderate depth — no HR risk, but triples are real.
gamePlan.tip: Washington has zero home runs on the season, so deep fly balls are not a concern. However, Roth (2 triples, ISO .375), Geheran (1 triple), Saifher (1 triple), and Adams (1 triple) all have gap-to-triple speed. Outfielders should position at slightly shallower-than-normal depth to cut off gap balls early, while still respecting the alleys. Do not play in shallow enough to give up the gap; the sweet spot is moderate depth favoring the alleys.

gamePlan.heading: Shade the outfield gaps, not the pull-line walls.
gamePlan.tip: With 14 doubles and 5 triples but no HRs, Washington lives in the gaps. CF and corner OFs should favor alleys over foul lines. The most common extra-base outcome is a ball hit between outfielders — positioning the center fielder slightly toward either gap depending on the batter handedness will cut off the most dangerous hits.

gamePlan.heading: Priority: strand runners from the top of the order before Geheran and Adams bat.
gamePlan.tip: Washington's lineup is structured so that Sison (7 R, +6 R_diff), Matsurra (8 R, +4 R_diff), Poucher (6 R, +3 R_diff), and Roth (+5 R_diff) all function as lead-off types who get on base and score. Retiring those table-setters before Geheran (.739, 15 RBI, 0.88 RBI/H) and Adams (.700, 1.00 RBI/H) bat is the single highest-leverage defensive priority. Hold baserunners aggressively and prioritize limiting their on-base opportunities.

gamePlan.heading: Play the infield honest — no power shifts needed, but stay ready for hard contact up the middle.
gamePlan.tip: With zero HRs, no dramatic pull-side shifts are warranted. The team hits for contact at a .546 team AVG, meaning hard grounders and line drives up the middle are common. Infield should play standard depth with slight shading toward the middle to handle the contact-heavy lineup. Expect fewer slow rollers and more sharp ground balls.

gamePlan.heading: Attack the bottom of the lineup early and conserve pitching energy for the middle.
gamePlan.tip: Sison (.316 AVG, 2-for-9 recent), Ciccarelli (.312 AVG), and Sandell (.462 AVG) are the most manageable outs in the lineup. However, Ciccarelli has a 1.00 RBI/H ratio — do not leave pitches in the zone with runners on even against lower-average hitters. The goal is to get quick outs from the 9-11 spots to face a smaller lineup and reduce Geheran's, Adams's, and Mello's at-bats with runners on base.

burlingame-expansion.summaryNote: Burlingame Expansion stumbled to a 1-4 start but capped the first half of the season with a statement 26-10 blowout of Franklin in week 7 — a performance that signals this team is capable of erupting offensively when everything clicks. The Gallant brothers anchor a dangerous top of the order: Nolan is an elite extra-base threat with a staggering .786 ISO driven by 3 triples and a home run, while Vic makes consistent contact at .818 AVG. Do not let their record lull you into complacency — they can put up a crooked number in a hurry.
burlingame-expansion.lineupNote: The team rotates a roster of roughly 11-12, with the Gallant brothers, Camacho, and Lasky logging the most appearances; Armanini has been dangerous in limited games, and Jack Maguire (3-for-3, 3 RBI in week 7) is an emerging wildcard off the bench.

lineup.tip: The most dangerous bat on this roster. Nolan's .786 ISO is historically elite for this league — his 3 triples and 1 HR out of 9 hits means almost half his hits go for extra bases. He went 8-for-11 over the last 3 games and racked up 8 runs scored. In the week 7 Franklin blowout he was clearly one of the engines of the 26-run outburst. He has gap-to-gap power AND the speed to turn doubles into triples; the outfield must play extremely deep whenever he steps in.
lineup.pitchTip: Pitch low and inside to limit extension; avoid anything belt-high in the middle third of the plate. Change speeds aggressively — he has elite bat speed and will pull anything predictable. Do not give him a first-pitch fastball over the plate.

lineup.tip: Vic leads all Expansion players in batting average at .818 and is arguably the hardest to retire on a pure contact basis. His 7-for-8 performance over the last 3 games shows he is absolutely locked in. With a .273 ISO he also has extra-base pop — 1 double and 1 triple in 9 hits. Batting alongside his brother Nolan, the two create a lethal 1-2 punch at the top of the order that can open innings wide open.
lineup.pitchTip: Keep him off-balance with off-speed pitches; he appears to be a gap hitter who likes to go the other way. Jamming him inside may be your best option — do not pitch him away where he can extend. Do not let him see a pattern.

lineup.tip: Camacho is one of the team's two home run hitters and pairs elite average (.615) with genuine power (.308 ISO). He has driven in 5 runs while scoring 5 — a balanced threat who cleans up runners effectively. His RBI/H ratio of 0.62 means runners in scoring position will come home against him. He went 5-for-10 in his last 3 games, suggesting a slight dip from his season mark that has not cost him productivity.
lineup.pitchTip: He has HR power — keep everything down in the zone. Do not leave anything elevated. His 1 HR and high ISO suggest he can drive the ball to any field; do not give him anything to pull on the inner half.

lineup.tip: Armanini has only appeared in 3 games but has been virtually automatic at the plate, hitting .833 with a 5-for-6 showing in recent games. His sample is small but the contact rate is impossible to dismiss — he has not shown power (ISO .000) but with a hit rate this high, he is a guaranteed on-base threat every at-bat. Teams will likely increase his role given his output.
lineup.pitchTip: Work him with movement — he appears to be a pure contact hitter with no power, so keep pitches just off the corners to induce weak contact. Do not walk him; put the ball in play and trust your defense.

lineup.tip: Murphy has quietly hit .600 over 4 games and is 5-for-8 in his last 3, showing consistent contact throughout the season. He has 1 double and 3 RBI, making him a reliable run producer in the middle of the order. His +1 R_diff indicates he scores slightly more than he drives in, suggesting he gets on base and lets the lineup behind him do work.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a contact hitter with moderate RBI production — pitch him away and down to induce ground balls. Do not work him inside where a pull hitter can drive runs in; keep him honest with off-speed pitches.

lineup.tip: Lasky is the team's most consistent RBI machine — his 0.86 RBI/H ratio is second-best on the team among multi-game players. In 5 games he has driven in 6 runs and hit .500 with no extra-base hits, meaning almost every hit he gets is productive. His -1 R_diff tells you he drives others in more than he scores himself — he is batting in a run-producing slot. He went 4-for-9 in his last 3 games, a slight recent dip, but he remains clutch with runners on.
lineup.pitchTip: He produces runs purely through contact, not power — work him with offspeed pitches in the dirt to induce chases. Try to keep runners off base ahead of him; if bases are loaded, treat him like a power threat despite his zero ISO.

lineup.tip: Jauregui is the team's best table setter — he scores 6 runs against only 2 RBI, a +4 R_diff that leads all Expansion players. He gets on base and creates chaos, particularly over the last few weeks where he went 4-for-8. With the Gallant brothers and Camacho hitting behind him, his on-base ability translates directly into runs. He is not a power threat (ISO .067) but he is difficult to keep off base.
lineup.pitchTip: Get him out early in the count — he is a table setter who thrives on working counts. Attack him with first-pitch strikes and do not give him free bases; every time he reaches base he creates scoring opportunities for the dangerous hitters behind him.

lineup.tip: Marguilies hits for a lower average but punches above his weight in run production — 0.75 RBI/H means three out of every four hits drives a run home. His 4-for-9 showing over the last 3 games suggests recent consistency despite a modest season line. With 1 double in 4 hits, he can gap the ball when needed.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a situational RBI bat — keep runners off base ahead of him and pitch to his weak average rather than fearing his power. Low pitches away should generate weak contact from a hitter who thrives with runners on.

lineup.tip: Kraska's 1.00 RBI/H ratio is the best on the team among players with significant at-bats — every single one of his 4 hits this season has driven in a run. He has 2 doubles and has gone 4-for-8 recently, showing consistent extra-base pop. His -4 R_diff (0 runs scored, 4 RBI) tells you he is a pure cleanup-type bat who drives others in and rarely scores himself, suggesting he bats deep in the order.
lineup.pitchTip: With a 1.00 RBI/H ratio, treat him as a guaranteed RBI machine when runners are on. Do not let him see a pitch he can drive in the air — work him down in the zone. His .182 ISO suggests he is a gap hitter; keep the ball inside to prevent him from extending.

lineup.tip: Soto has 4 hits and 2 runs scored in 4 games but has driven in zero runs, suggesting he bats at the top of the order or in a lead-off role. His 3-for-7 last 3 games is serviceable. He poses no power threat (ISO .000) and his value is entirely in getting on base and creating opportunities for the bigger bats behind him.
lineup.pitchTip: He has zero extra-base power — work him with offspeed and keep pitches out of the fat part of the zone. Attack early in the count; he is not a patient hitter who will punish a pitcher's mistake with extra bases.

lineup.tip: Maguire appeared only in week 7 against Franklin and was perfect: 3-for-3 with 3 RBI. Small sample, but his debut coincided with the team's only win — a 26-10 blowout — and he made an immediate impact. His role going forward is unclear, but if he appears he is fully capable of producing immediately without a warm-up period.
lineup.pitchTip: Unknown quantities are dangerous — treat him with respect. His 3 RBI in one game suggest he drives the ball with runners on. Mix your pitches and do not groove anything over the plate until you have a read on his swing tendencies.

players.tip: The most dangerous hitter on this roster by a wide margin. Nolan's .786 ISO is extraordinary — he has 3 triples and 1 HR in just 9 hits across 14 at-bats. His 8-for-11 stretch over the last 3 games shows he is peaking at exactly the right moment. Any pitcher who challenges him in the zone risks a ball leaving the field or rattling the outfield wall. Play the outfield at maximum depth.

Camacho is the second home run threat on Expansion and combines elite average with real power. His .308 ISO is the second highest on the team; he has driven in 5 runs in 4 games and scores at the same rate. Expect him to be batted in the heart of the order — do not pitch around him carelessly when the lineup is clicking.

Vic hits for elite average and has enough ISO to gap the ball for doubles and triples. He does not rely on home run power but drives the ball into the alleys consistently, making deep outfield alignment important even for him.

Both of Kraska's extra-base hits are doubles and his 1.00 RBI/H makes every extra-base opportunity a run-scoring event. He bats deep in the order and turns his gap shots into RBIs. Keep him from seeing pitches he can loft to the alleys.

Nolan's 3 triples are the most on the team by a large margin and are the primary driver of his elite ISO. He has the combination of bat speed and running speed to turn deep fly balls into triples. The outfield must play at maximum depth to have any chance of cutting him off.
Vic also has a triple on his season line. Less of a triples threat than Nolan but should be respected in the outfield — do not play shallow on either Gallant.

Appeared only in week 7 against Franklin (the team's first win) and went 3-for-3 with 3 RBI. Unknown quantities with this kind of debut are dangerous — if he appears in your game, do not underestimate him.
Armanini has played only 3 games but is hitting .833 across them. If he increases his appearances, he immediately becomes one of the most dangerous contact bats on the team.
Drives in a run every time he gets a hit. With 4 RBI on 4 hits and 2 doubles, he is a prototypical run-production bat — effective when runners are on base.
Team leader in RBI with 6 in 5 games; his 0.86 RBI/H ratio is elite for a no-power hitter. He converts contact into runs scored with remarkable efficiency — keep runners off base ahead of him.
Three of his four hits drove in runs. He is a reliable situational producer despite a modest overall line.

sections.title: Table Setters (score more than they drive in)

players.tip: The best table setter on Expansion — he scores 3x as many runs as he drives in. He gets on base, stays out of double plays, and creates opportunities for the Gallants and Camacho. Keeping him off base is a priority.

Nolan scores at a remarkable rate (8 runs in 4 games) while also driving in 5. His +3 R_diff reflects how often he reaches base and turns extra-base hits into runs. He is both a table setter and a run producer simultaneously.
Soto has zero RBI but has scored twice — a pure table setter who gets on base and relies on others to drive him home. His presence at the top of the order means the lineup is built to produce.

gamePlan.heading: Play the outfield at maximum depth for Nolan Gallant.
gamePlan.tip: Nolan has 3 triples and a HR in just 14 at-bats — .786 ISO. Any ball he hits to the outfield gaps has extra-base potential. Corner outfielders should shade toward the alleys and start at maximum depth. A single to shallow right is preferable to a triple to the right-center gap.

gamePlan.heading: Neutralize the Gallant brothers by limiting back-to-back damage.
gamePlan.tip: Nolan and Vic together have 18 hits, 13 runs, and 8 RBI across 4 games. When they hit consecutively in the order, a single hit from each translates into a run. Prioritize retiring the first Gallant before the other comes up with runners on — do not let them feed each other in the same inning.

gamePlan.heading: Treat the week-7 momentum as real — this team is dangerous at full strength.
gamePlan.tip: The 26-10 win over Franklin is not a fluke of the schedule. All their key bats came alive at once and the run total shows a team that can explode. Do not look only at the 1-4 record; their week-7 form is the more predictive sample of what this lineup is capable of.

gamePlan.heading: Keep runners off base ahead of Lasky and Kraska.
gamePlan.tip: Lasky (0.86 RBI/H, 6 RBI) and Kraska (1.00 RBI/H, 4 RBI) are automatic run converters. If the Gallants and Camacho load the bases, these two will cash them in. Prevent their big bats from doing work by retiring the top of the order efficiently.

gamePlan.heading: Scout Maguire before the game — he is an unknown wildcard.
gamePlan.tip: Jack Maguire went 3-for-3 with 3 RBI in his only appearance (week 7, the 26-10 win). Zero prior history means no tendencies to exploit. If he starts, pitch him early-count fastballs away and look for any swing pattern before adjusting; do not groove a ball over the plate on the first at-bat.

roosevelt-blue.summaryNote: Roosevelt Blue is a 2-3 rebuilding squad that has shown genuine offensive punch in bursts -- their 18-6 demolition of Carey in week 4 demonstrated what this lineup can do when everything clicks, but a 15-3 blowout loss to St. Catherines the following week exposed their inconsistency. Three separate players have gone yard (Shapiro, Ortega, Ding), meaning power is distributed rather than concentrated, and they closed the most recent week by beating Washington Wildkittens 9-6 to take 2 of their last 3. At a .491 team average they make contact, but a .621 slugging mark tells you most of that contact is singles -- gaps and extra bases will come from a handful of specific threats worth knowing by name.
roosevelt-blue.lineupNote: Roosevelt Blue carries an 11-player rotation with solid depth at the top; Vinca and Cockle provide a high-contact one-two punch, Adler and Shapiro offer the best blend of average and power, and Frank quietly leads the team in RBI despite modest peripherals.

lineup.tip: Adler is the most complete bat in this lineup -- .615 average over 13 AB with a triple, a double, and an ISO of .231 that ranks second on the team. He is 6-for-10 over the last three games, contributing in both the Carey blowout win and the Washington victory. Watch for him to work gaps; his triple is evidence he runs well and will challenge the outfield corners.
lineup.pitchTip: Keep the ball down and away; his extra-base hits suggest he covers the outer third well on flat pitches. Elevate to change his eye level and try to induce weak contact up in the zone.

lineup.tip: Vinca leads the team in hits (10) and runs (7) and is almost exclusively a table-setter -- a +4 R-to-RBI differential signals he scores far more than he drives in. He is 6-for-10 over his last three games and has been the most consistent at-bat through a tough stretch. His ISO of .118 means he is hitting singles and doubles, not barrels.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a contact hitter who punishes mistakes over the plate. Work him with off-speed and keep fastballs on the corners; do not groove anything middle-in. Getting him out early in the count limits his ability to put the ball in play repeatedly.

lineup.tip: Cockle has been remarkably consistent -- 9 hits in 16 AB over five games, currently 6-for-9 over his last three outings. His ISO of .062 and zero extra-base power beyond a single double make him purely a contact guy, but his even R/RBI split (+0 R_diff) means he both scores and contributes. He is unlikely to beat you alone but will strand runners if not retired.
lineup.pitchTip: He offers no real gap threat, so play your outfield shallower and concede nothing in the infield. Soft contact and ground balls are fine -- his ISO tells you he will not drive the ball far. Change speeds early to disrupt his timing.

lineup.tip: Ortega is the most dangerous RBI bat on the team relative to his hit count -- an .83 RBI/H ratio means nearly every hit produces a run scored by someone else. He has a .308 ISO (the team's best among multi-game players), a home run, and a double in 13 AB. His 6 runs and 5 RBI in just four games are quiet-dangerous numbers; he was likely a key contributor during the Carey 18-6 win.
lineup.pitchTip: Do not let him see anything elevated or middle-up with runners on base. His ISO and HR suggest he can get to a hanging pitch. Bust him inside early to jam him, then finish low and away to limit hard contact.

lineup.tip: Shapiro has the only traditional power profile in the top half of the order -- .500 average paired with a home run and a .688 slugging mark across five full games. He was 4-for-9 over his last three games, a minor dip from his season pace, but his ISO of .188 and solo homer keep him dangerous. His +2 R_diff suggests he hits in high-leverage moments.
lineup.pitchTip: His home run was likely on a pitch that stayed up or out over the plate. Work him low in the zone and change speeds; avoid anything belt-high on the outer half. He has seen five full games so his timing will be sharp -- do not challenge him early in an at-bat.

lineup.tip: Ding has played only three games but has been scorching -- 5-for-8 with a home run, a .625 average, and a .375 ISO that leads the entire roster. His 3 RBI in just 8 AB project to an elite pace. He is entirely hot right now and his limited sample means pitchers have no established book on him.
lineup.pitchTip: He has been seeing the ball exceptionally well (5-for-8, HR) with no recent cold stretch to exploit. Mix locations aggressively and avoid any predictable patterns -- he is a new name with no visible weakness yet. Test him inside early and see if he can adjust; do not give him anything to extend his arms on.

lineup.tip: Frank leads the team in RBI with 6 despite just 8 hits -- a .75 RBI/H ratio indicating he comes up in high-run-producing situations and delivers. His -4 R_diff tells you he rarely scores himself, likely batting in the middle-to-lower part of the order when runners are already on. He has a triple, showing he can gap the ball when he connects solidly.
lineup.pitchTip: Strand runners before he comes to the plate whenever possible -- his value is almost entirely context-dependent. With the bases clear he is much less dangerous (.471 AVG but no HR, low ISO). Attack early in the count and get him to make contact on your terms rather than his.

lineup.tip: Carvillo has a .545 average in 11 AB across four games, pairs two doubles with an ISO of .182, and scores at a high clip (+3 R_diff). He is 5-for-9 over his last three games and appears to set up damage for the middle of the lineup. His 6 runs in just four games puts him second on the team in that category.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a contact-oriented gap hitter who gets on base and lets others drive him in. Prioritize limiting his reach base rate -- anything on the outer half will be driven to the gaps. Work inner half to keep him off the plate and induce soft pull-side grounders.

lineup.tip: O'Leary is 6-for-10 over his last three games -- the hottest recent stretch on the team in raw terms -- yet his .000 ISO and -2 R_diff tell you all six of those hits are singles and he is consistently left on base. He has been extraordinarily contact-consistent but carries no power threat whatsoever.
lineup.pitchTip: He punishes the ball in play but cannot hit it over anyone's head. Shift the outfield in to take away soft singles and play the infield at normal depth. Strikeouts are ideal but hard contact that stays in the infield works just as well -- he will not barrel you.

lineup.tip: Bhargava hits for the lowest average on the roster (.286) but leads the entire team in RBI rate -- 1.25 RBI per hit, meaning almost every hit he gets produces multiple runs. His -4 R_diff mirrors Frank's profile: he drives people in but rarely scores himself. With runners on base he is more dangerous than his AVG suggests; his 5 RBI in 14 AB are likely clustered in big-inning situations.
lineup.pitchTip: Get him out with the bases empty and do not let runners reach before his at-bat if you can help it. His average is low enough (.286) that he will make outs -- just do not serve him a mistake with runners on. High and tight to disrupt his timing, then finish on the black away.

lineup.tip: Ganguly is the lightest bat in the rotation -- .333 average over 12 AB, one double, and an ISO of .083. His 3-for-8 last three games and even R_diff mark him as a reliable but unpunishing contact hitter. He is unlikely to change the complexion of a game on his own.
lineup.pitchTip: Standard approach -- work the corners and change speeds. He has shown no power, so a flyball out is as good as a strikeout. Do not overthink this at-bat; get ahead in the count and make him chase.

players.tip: In only 8 AB Ding has an ISO of .375 -- the highest on the roster. His home run in three games combined with a .625 average makes him an unresolved scouting mystery. He is the lone bat with both elite contact and true power in the same profile.

Leads the team in ISO (.308) among regular players, with a home run and double in 13 AB. Ortega is the most dangerous extra-base threat when on base; his .83 RBI/H means a hit nearly always scores someone.

Shapiro provides the most experienced power profile -- HR, five games of seasoning, .500 average. His ISO (.188) lags behind Ding and Ortega but he is the most battle-tested power bat and most likely to see meaningful at-bats in close games.

No home run but a triple and double give Adler a .231 ISO and the second-highest slugging on the team. He is the most consistent of the near-power bats and his triple signals genuine outfield-challenging speed.
Two doubles in 11 AB; Carvillo uses the whole field and punishes outfield mistakes. His .545 average keeps gaps honest and makes him one of the more well-rounded threats in the middle of the order.
Adler's gap production (double plus triple) alongside his high average makes him capable of turning singles situations into extra bases. Play outfield corners honest against him.

Two doubles in 17 AB suggest Vinca uses the gaps to extend his already-high contact rate. With the speed implied by a +4 R_diff, he will turn gap singles into doubles when the outfield plays too deep.
Only player on the roster with a triple; Adler will challenge right-center and left-center gaps and has the speed to leg out extra bases. Do not loaf on balls hit in the alleys when he is up.

Frank's triple is a reminder that he can pull the ball hard or drive it in the gap despite modest peripherals. Outfield depth matters when he is up with the bases empty -- a triple here becomes a tying or go-ahead run with one swing.
Ding has the highest ISO on the team in just 8 AB -- barely scouted, batting well over .600, with a home run. He is the most under-the-radar danger in this lineup.
Carvillo scores at nearly 1.5 runs per game played -- only 4 appearances but already second on the team in runs. He has a higher floor than his modest hit total suggests.

Bhargava's 1.25 RBI/H ratio is the best on the team by a wide margin -- when he connects he is almost always driving in multiple runners. His .286 average means he makes plenty of outs, but do not let him see a pitch to hit with runners in scoring position.

Ortega combines the team's best ISO with an .83 RBI/H rate, making him the most complete RBI threat. He hits for extra bases and drives runners home -- the most dangerous combination in cleanup situations.

Frank leads the team in RBI despite no home runs -- purely a situational RBI machine. His .75 RBI/H and a triple indicate he is hitting into gap situations with runners on base. Do not serve him a mistake with runners on.

sections.title: Table Setters (score more than they drive in)

players.tip: Vinca leads the team in runs (7) and leads all table-setters in R_diff (+4). His 10 hits in 17 AB get him on base constantly, and he regularly turns singles into runs via the middle of the order. Getting him out in his first at-bat sets the tone for the inning.

Carvillo scores in nearly every game he plays (6 R in 4 G) and is clearly batting near the top of a productive lineup. His +3 R_diff makes him the second-best table-setter on the team -- get him out and you disrupt their run-scoring chain.

Adler's +2 R_diff paired with his .615 average and gap power means he reaches base and scores more often than he drives in -- a table-setter who also punishes mistakes for extra bases. He is the most versatile threat in their lineup.

gamePlan.heading: Neutralize the top of the order early.
gamePlan.tip: Vinca (.588, 10 H) and Cockle (.562, 9 H) have been on-base machines -- both are 6-for-9 or 6-for-10 in their last three games. Getting two quick outs before they reach changes the entire inning calculus; if either reaches, expect Adler (.615) or Shapiro (.500, 1 HR) to drive them in.

gamePlan.heading: Shade the outfield for Ortega, Ding, and Adler.
gamePlan.tip: These three account for all three team home runs and both triples, with ISOs of .308, .375, and .231 respectively. Play the outfield corners deep when any of them are up with runners on; a gap double here converts to 2 RBI at their .83, .60, and .25 RBI/H rates.

gamePlan.heading: Manage Frank and Bhargava with the bases empty.
gamePlan.tip: Frank (.75 RBI/H, 6 RBI) and Bhargava (1.25 RBI/H, 5 RBI) are situational RBI threats, not on-base machines. Both have negative R_diff (-4 each), meaning they rarely score themselves. Force them to the plate with nobody on and their RBI threat drops dramatically -- they have to do all the work alone.

gamePlan.heading: Exploit their big-inning volatility -- keep the game tight early.
gamePlan.tip: Roosevelt Blue crushed Carey 18-6 (week 4) but got blasted 15-3 by St. Catherines (week 5), suggesting a lineup that either erupts as a unit or collapses. They beat Washington 9-6 most recently and carry modest momentum, but this is not a battle-tested team. Keeping the score within two runs through three innings historically has pressured this type of streaky offense into low-output innings.

gamePlan.heading: Target the lower third (Bhargava, Ganguly) for quick innings.
gamePlan.tip: Bhargava (.286) and Ganguly (.333) are the two lowest-average regulars; combined they have 8 hits in 26 AB and zero home runs. Their ISOs (.000 and .083) mean soft contact is fine -- any out here prevents the middle of the order from seeing a big-RBI situation. Do not walk either one into position for Vinca or Adler to come up with runners on.

carey.summaryNote: Carey sits at 1-4 but their record undersells a roster loaded with contact hitters — they nearly upset Washington in week 1, losing by a single run 14-13, and their lone win came against Burlingame-Expansion 10-7. Several players carry alarming ISO in limited samples: O'Hare posts a 1.000 ISO (1 HR, 2 triples in just 7 AB) and Batenchuch sits at .600 ISO from 3 doubles in only 5 AB, making the bottom of their lineup potentially the most dangerous part. Their blowout losses to Franklin (20-8) and Roosevelt-Blue (18-6) suggest inconsistency rather than outright weakness, and a deep rotating roster means fresh bats can appear in any game.
carey.lineupNote: Carey dresses 12-15 players with heavy game-to-game rotation, meaning dangerous part-time bats like Haugen, Batenchuch, and O'Hare can surface unpredictably — do not overlook anyone in the lower third of this lineup.

lineup.tip: O'Hare is the single biggest threat on this roster in terms of raw power. His 1.000 ISO from 7 AB (1 HR, 2 triples) is a major outlier — he hit one HR against Hoover in week 7 and has multi-base hits in nearly every game he appears. With 3 R and 2 RBI already, he does real damage in limited appearances.
lineup.pitchTip: Keep everything low and away; he has demonstrated he can drive elevated pitches over the fence and pull gap shots into triples. Do not let him get an inside pitch he can extend on.

lineup.tip: Batenchuch has the second-highest ISO on the team at .600, built entirely on doubles — 3 in just 5 AB — giving him a .800 AVG and a +3 R differential. He went 4-for-5 in his last three games and has shown he can turn on any pitch into the gaps. Small sample but every AB counts.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a pure gap hitter right now. Pitch him away and down, and shade your outfield deep toward the alleys. Do not let him see a belt-high pitch middle-away.

lineup.tip: Acton leads the team in hits (8) and is their most consistent table-setter — 7 R against only 2 RBI signals he scores far more than he drives in, making him the catalyst at the top of the order. His .250 ISO (3 doubles in 12 AB) shows he has gap power, and he went 5-for-9 over his last three games including the near-upset of Washington.
lineup.pitchTip: Acton is a contact machine — do not nibble. Challenge him with hard stuff away and force weak contact. Getting him out early changes the inning dynamic since he ignites their offense.

lineup.tip: Barabin is in scorching recent form — 6-for-7 over his last three games, the hottest streak on the team. He carries a .700 season average with 5 R and 4 RBI in 10 AB, and his +1 R differential indicates he hits in traffic. He was productive in both the near-miss against Washington and the win over Burlingame.
lineup.pitchTip: Do not give him anything comfortable — he is seeing the ball extremely well right now. Work him hard away and try to get him to roll over on a low pitch. Avoid leaving anything in the middle of the zone.

lineup.tip: Haugen has the highest AVG on the team at .833 in 2 games, going 5-for-6 in his last three games while posting an 0.80 RBI/H ratio — he drives runners in at an elite rate. His -3 R differential means he tends to bat with runners on and cash them rather than score himself. Dangerous RBI bat who shows up when it matters.
lineup.pitchTip: Haugen is a run-producer, not a table-setter — the situation when he comes up will be critical. Pitch around him if the bases are loaded with two outs; otherwise work him low and inside to induce a ground ball.

lineup.tip: Coleman is an elite run producer in limited looks — 4 RBI in just 7 AB with a .714 average. His 0.80 RBI/H ties Haugen for the run-producing title on the roster. With only a .143 ISO he does not hit for extra bases often, but his ability to come through with runners on makes him one of the most clutch bats in the lineup.
lineup.pitchTip: Coleman thrives with runners on. Pitch him away and try to get soft contact — he does not have significant extra-base power so a ground ball to the right side is your best case. Do not groove anything.

lineup.tip: Chow is their most complete hitter across a full schedule — 7 H in 13 AB over 5 games with 1 HR, 1 double, 4 RBI, and a .308 ISO. He is the only multi-game regular with meaningful extra-base power alongside contact, and his even R differential (+0) means he both scores and drives in runs. He went 5-for-8 over his last three games.
lineup.pitchTip: Chow has legitimate home run pop — keep the ball down and avoid hanging breaking balls. He is their most disciplined power bat, so do not try to blow elevated fastballs by him.

lineup.tip: Colaco has a perfect 1.00 RBI/H ratio — every hit he gets drives in a run. His .400 ISO (1 triple in 5 AB) shows gap-to-gap power in small sample. With 3 RBI in just 5 AB he is quietly one of the most dangerous run-producing bats when he plays, and his -2 R differential confirms he is used as a deep RBI bat.
lineup.pitchTip: Treat Colaco like a clean-up hitter even if he bats lower in the order. Pitch around him with runners in scoring position if you can afford it; if not, work low and away and hope for a flyout rather than a triple.

lineup.tip: Wicks is a pure contact and speed threat — .714 average, 5-for-7 over his last three games, zero extra-base hits but a +3 R differential showing he gets on base and scores consistently. He creates chaos at the top of the order by simply reaching base at an elite clip and then putting pressure on the defense.
lineup.pitchTip: Wicks has no ISO so there is no extra-base threat, but his contact rate is exceptional. Throw him hard stuff with movement and make him hit it into the ground — he is not going to beat you with power but he will beat you by reaching base every time.

lineup.tip: Wilkinson has produced in limited playing time — .667 average in 2 games, 4-for-6 over his last three games, with 2 RBI and an 0.50 RBI/H ratio. His -1 R differential suggests he bats in the middle of the order and produces in traffic rather than setting the table.
lineup.pitchTip: Wilkinson has shown a .167 ISO (one double) so there is some gap threat. Work him away with off-speed pitches and keep the ball out of the heart of the zone.

lineup.tip: Jewett is a pure singles hitter with zero ISO but solid contact at .556 in 9 AB. He went 4-for-7 over his last three games and has a +1 R differential, meaning he does his job as a table-setter consistently. He was productive during the Burlingame win.
lineup.pitchTip: No extra-base threat at all — pitch him aggressively in the zone and look for soft contact. Infield shift is a viable option given his ground ball tendency.

lineup.tip: Barr is a part-time contributor with a modest .400 average in 10 AB but a +2 R differential — he scores runs when he reaches. One double in 10 AB shows minimal extra-base power. He contributes most when used as a table-setter rather than a run-producer.
lineup.pitchTip: Barr is the least threatening regular in the lineup. Pitch him standard stuff in the zone and let your defense work. Get the out and move on.

players.tip: O'Hare is a small-sample monster — his 1.000 ISO is the highest on the team and one of the most dangerous figures in the league. Three extra-base hits in 7 AB including a home run against Hoover in week 7. He does not play every game but when he does, he has multi-base hit upside in any at-bat.

Batenchuch has turned 3 of his 4 hits into doubles, producing a .600 ISO in 5 AB. His .800 average and +3 R differential make him dangerous at the top of any lineup spot. Appeared in the Burlingame win and was a major factor.
Chow is the only regular starter with a HR and a sustained .308 ISO across 5 games. He is the most durable power bat on the roster — available every game and capable of going yard.
Three doubles in 5 AB — he is beating the shift into the alleys consistently.
Acton has 3 doubles in 12 AB, leading all regulars in doubles. He reads the gap well and routinely turns singles into doubles.
Barabin has gap power to complement his elite contact rate — 2 doubles in 10 AB and in the best form on the team right now.
O'Hare has hit 2 triples in just 7 AB — the most alarming triple threat on this roster. His combination of HR and triple power makes him uniquely dangerous at any base count.
Colaco hit a triple in 5 AB along with his strong RBI production — suggests he has enough speed and bat to reach the gaps.
Only 3 games in but already has a HR and 2 triples. If O'Hare becomes a regular starter, he becomes the most dangerous bat on this team instantly.
Two games in and already 3 doubles — Batenchuch is a part-time bat who can change a game the moment he enters the lineup. Do not overlook him on the bench.
Haugen is 5-for-6 in limited appearances with 4 RBI. His RBI/H ratio of .80 makes him a threat the moment he enters the game as a pinch hitter or substitute starter.
Colaco has driven in a run on every single hit this season — a perfect 1.00 RBI/H in 5 AB. He bats with runners on and consistently delivers.
Coleman has 4 RBI in just 7 AB — he appears to bat in high-leverage spots and delivers. His .714 average compounds the run-production threat significantly.
Haugen matches Coleman with a 0.80 RBI/H ratio and 4 RBI in only 6 hits. His -3 R differential confirms he bats deep with runners on — a classic clean-up role.

sections.title: Table Setters (score more than they drive in)

players.tip: Acton is their best leadoff option — 7 R and only 2 RBI is the largest positive differential on the team. He reaches base, advances, and scores with elite consistency. He was on base repeatedly during the near-miss against Washington.
Wicks scores 3 times without a single RBI — a pure table-setter who gets on and lets others drive him home. His .714 average and zero extra-base hits define his role.
Despite his power numbers (.600 ISO), Batenchuch scores more than he drives in — 4 R to 1 RBI in 5 AB. When he leads off an inning with a double, Carey tends to score.

gamePlan.heading: Shade the outfield deep for O'Hare and Batenchuch.
gamePlan.tip: O'Hare has 2 triples and 1 HR in 7 AB (1.000 ISO) and Batenchuch has 3 doubles in 5 AB (.600 ISO). Both players can drive the ball to all fields with authority. When either steps in, pull your outfielders back and toward the gaps — giving up a single is far better than a triple or an inside-the-park HR.

gamePlan.heading: Neutralize the run-production core (Colaco, Coleman, Haugen) with runners on base.
gamePlan.tip: All three post RBI/H ratios of .80 or higher — Colaco at 1.00, Coleman and Haugen at .80. These bats thrive in high-leverage at-bats. When Carey has runners at second or third with fewer than two outs, pitch away from these three or accept the walk to face a weaker bat.

gamePlan.heading: Disrupt Acton and Wicks at the top of the order to cut off the run-scoring chain.
gamePlan.tip: Acton (+5 R vs RBI) and Wicks (+3 R vs RBI) are Carey's ignition. Acton leads the team with 8 H across 4 games and is 5-for-9 in his last three. Getting both out in the first inning consistently will suppress their offense before the run-producers even bat.

gamePlan.heading: Exploit Carey's inconsistency — they were blown out twice (20-8, 18-6) but won 10-7.
gamePlan.tip: Carey gave up 20 runs to Franklin and 18 to Roosevelt-Blue, suggesting their defense and pitching can be punished with aggressive base running and gap hitting. Their lone win came by 3 runs against Burlingame-Expansion. Push the tempo early and force defensive mistakes — they crack under sustained offensive pressure.

gamePlan.heading: Respect the small-sample danger bats rotating in and out of the lineup.
gamePlan.tip: O'Hare (3G), Batenchuch (2G), Haugen (2G), and Wilkinson (2G) are all part-time players with elite stats in limited appearances. Do not let familiarity with the Carey lineup become complacency — a fresh bat entering in the fourth inning can have a .800 average and 4 RBI on the season. Always check who is newly in the lineup and adjust accordingly.

mckinley-2.summaryNote: McKinley 2 sits at 1-3-1 but the record flatters to deceive — they lost to Washington Wildkittens by a single run in week 4 and battled Lincoln Lions to a 14-14 tie in week 7, showing they can hang with the league's better squads. Brandon Wright is the engine of the offense, slashing .786 over five games with a blistering 9-for-10 stretch across his last three, and Chris Corde announced himself in the week 7 tie with a jaw-dropping 5 RBI on 2 hits including a home run in just 3 at-bats. If Corde is in the lineup, treat him as a top-three threat regardless of the modest team record.
mckinley-2.lineupNote: McKinley 2 dresses 11-12 players with relatively consistent rotation; Wright and Rodriguez anchor the top of the order while Johnston and Corde provide mid-lineup pop when available.

lineup.tip: Wright is McKinley 2's most reliable bat, going 11-for-14 on the season with an ISO of .286 and 6 runs scored. He is currently on a 9-for-10 tear over his last three games and has been productive in every game including the week 4 near-upset of Washington (.786 is the team high among full-time starters). His R_diff of +2 shows he scores at roughly the same rate he reaches, so he manufactures runs as well as drives them.
lineup.pitchTip: Attack early in the count — he makes contact on everything. Keep pitches low and away to limit hard contact; do not groove anything belt-high or he will drive it. Mixing speeds is the best disruption tool.

lineup.tip: Corde only appeared in one game — the week 7 tie with Lincoln Lions — but posted 2 hits, 1 HR, and 5 RBI in just 3 at-bats, an extraordinary ISO of 1.333 and 2.50 RBI/H. His R_diff of -3 means nearly all his plate appearances end with runners scoring; he is a pure run-producer. Small sample size, but the performance was not fluky — he clearly has legitimate pop.
lineup.pitchTip: Do not let him get extended on anything inside. Pitch him away consistently and make him reach for it; a player with this much raw power will chase if you establish the outside corner early. Never throw him anything elevated.

lineup.tip: Parikh leads the team in batting average at .833 (5-for-6) in three games and has not recorded an RBI yet, meaning he is primarily a table-setter who gets on base at an elite clip. His ISO of .167 is modest, but his contact rate is exceptional. Watch for him to appear in more games as the season progresses — his 5-for-6 three-game stretch is entirely his season, so he has no cold stretches on record.
lineup.pitchTip: He has not driven in a run all season — he is a contact hitter, not a power bat. Pitch him to make weak contact; he is unlikely to go deep but almost certain to put the ball in play, so your defense needs to be alert when he is up.

lineup.tip: Dabrik went 7-for-9 over his last three games and owns a .700 average on the season with 5 RBI — tied for second on the team — and an RBI/H ratio of .71, qualifying him as a legitimate run producer. Two doubles show he can hit for some gap power (ISO .200). His R_diff of -3 is the second-worst on the team, meaning runners score at a high rate when he comes up.
lineup.pitchTip: Keep the ball on the ground — his doubles suggest a level, line-drive swing. Avoid leaving anything middle-away; pound him inside to get him to pull weakly or jam him.

lineup.tip: Rodriguez has appeared in all five games and posts a .583 average with 5 RBI and 5 runs, making him one of the team's most complete offensive contributors. His RBI/H ratio of .71 ranks among the team's run producers, and two doubles indicate gap power. He is the most experienced and consistent threat in the lineup after Wright, showing up in the close week 4 loss and the week 7 tie alike.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a balanced hitter — solid average with gap power but no HR. Use breaking balls early to disrupt his timing and avoid throwing straight fastballs on the outer half; he appears to drive those for doubles.

lineup.tip: Johnston has a .75 RBI/H ratio — highest among full-season regulars — going 4-for-8 with 3 RBI in three games. His zero ISO suggests pure contact, but his run-production rate is elite: when he gets a hit, runners score. His R_diff of -2 confirms he drives in more than he scores, so he bats with runners on base frequently.
lineup.pitchTip: He has zero extra-base hits but runners score when he singles, suggesting he hits to gaps or is well-placed in the lineup behind faster runners. Pitch carefully with runners on; a routine single can be costly. Challenge him to pull the ball by working inside.

lineup.tip: Anguera is a gap threat — his one triple and .75 RBI/H ratio suggest he can clear the bases when he gets hold of one. Four hits in 11 at-bats is modest, but three RBI and three runs scored in four games means he contributes across the board. He featured in the week 4 near-upset of Washington and in the week 7 tie.
lineup.pitchTip: His triple indicates he can drive the ball into the gaps; shade your outfielders toward the alleys when he bats. Pound him early with hard stuff inside to prevent him from extending his arms and going gap.

lineup.tip: Conti scores far more than he drives in — 4 runs against just 1 RBI across five games gives him a +3 R_diff, the second-best table-setter differential on the team. He goes to bat regularly (11 AB) and hits .545, making him a consistent on-base presence who creates opportunities for the lineup behind him.
lineup.pitchTip: Treat him as a table-setter: getting him out quickly matters more than striking him out, because the runners he scores come from the hitters behind him. Pitch him to induce weak ground balls and limit his on-base rate.

lineup.tip: Williams leads the team with a +4 R_diff — he scored 5 runs against just 1 RBI across five games, the clearest table-setter profile on the roster. He has appeared in every game and hits .417 with a single double, showing he is consistently on base. His 5-for-9 stretch over his last three games confirms he is staying on base at a high rate recently.
lineup.pitchTip: He is a pure runner — keep him off base and you neutralize his contribution entirely. Pitch him aggressively early in the count; do not walk him. If he gets on, watch for him to move aggressively on the bases.

lineup.tip: Whittier posts a .333 ISO — second-highest on the team after Corde among players with meaningful ABs — powered by two doubles and a triple in 12 at-bats. His .500 average and gap-power profile make him a legitimate extra-base threat. He appeared in the close week 4 loss to Washington and his triple suggests he can take an extra base aggressively.
lineup.pitchTip: His ISO is driven by extra-base hits, not HRs, so he is pulling the ball or going to the gaps. Play your outfield deep and slightly toward the gaps. Pitch him inside early to limit extension; he is more dangerous when he can get his arms out.

lineup.tip: Sparhawk has appeared in four games going 3-for-10 with 2 RBI and zero extra-base hits. His contribution is modest — an even RBI/H of .67 — but he is a consistent presence in the lineup. His R_diff of 0 means he is neither a runner nor a driver, sitting squarely in the middle of the lineup by role.
lineup.pitchTip: No extra-base hits and no ISO means he is a singles hitter. Pitch him up in the zone or way outside — make him work for contact. He is unlikely to do serious damage on his own.

players.tip: Wright is the team's top power-contact hybrid: .786 average with a .286 ISO and 1 HR across 14 at-bats. He is currently red-hot (9-for-10 last 3 games) and is the most consistent bat on the roster across all five games played.

Corde has the highest ISO on the team by a massive margin at 1.333 — his 1 HR and 5 RBI in just 3 at-bats during the week 7 tie with Lincoln Lions represents the most explosive single-game performance on the team this season. Treat him as a cleanup-level threat.

Whittier owns the second-highest ISO among regular starters at .333, producing 2 doubles and a triple in 12 at-bats. His extra-base hit rate (3 XBH in 12 AB = 25%) is the best on the team outside of Corde's one-game sample.
Dabrik's two doubles and .700 average make him a dangerous gap hitter who hits the ball hard and consistently. His 7-for-9 last-three-games stretch suggests he is timing pitches well right now.
Rodriguez pairs consistent contact (.583 AVG across 5 games) with gap power from two doubles, making him a reliable threat to drive runners in from scoring position.
Anguera's triple and ISO of .182 place him in the gap-hitter tier — he can take the ball the other way or pull it for extra bases, and he scores at a similar rate to his RBI production.

Whittier is one of two players on the roster with a triple this season, and his overall .333 ISO shows the triple was not an accident — he hits the ball with authority and runs well enough to stretch hits.
Anguera also has a triple and has scored 3 runs in 4 games, showing he is a threat to take an extra base and has the speed to score from second on singles.

That is a 2.50 RBI/H ratio and 1.333 ISO, both the highest on the team by a significant margin. If he is in the lineup, he belongs in your top-3 concerns regardless of the limited sample size. Do not pitch to him carelessly.

Corde's 2.50 RBI/H is nearly the entire team in a single game — every time he gets a hit, multiple runners score. The highest RBI/H on the roster by an extreme margin.
Johnston's .75 RBI/H is the highest among multi-game regulars, driving in 3 runs on 4 hits across three games. He is a pure run-producer who consistently bats with runners on base.

sections.title: Table Setters (score more than they drive in)

players.tip: Williams leads the team in R_diff at +4, scoring 5 runs against just 1 RBI across all five games. He is the primary table-setter — he gets on base and lets the lineup behind him do the damage. His 5-for-9 last-three-games form means he is currently getting on base at a high rate.

Conti also scores far more than he drives in (+3 R_diff over 5 games), batting .545 and getting on base consistently. He and Williams together form a two-player table-setting unit at the top of the order that the run-producing middle of the lineup feeds off.

gamePlan.heading: Neutralize Wright early — he is scorching hot.
gamePlan.tip: Wright is 9-for-10 over his last three games with a .786 season average and 1 HR. He makes consistent hard contact, so pitch him low and away early in the count to avoid letting him get extended. Do not groove fastballs belt-high; he will punish them. Getting him out in the first at-bat sets a tone for the whole game.

gamePlan.heading: Treat Corde as a cleanup hitter if he is in the lineup.
gamePlan.tip: Corde's one-game sample (5 RBI, 1 HR, 1.333 ISO in the week 7 tie vs Lincoln) is not noise — it is a signal. He has legitimate power and a dangerous swing. Pitch him away consistently, never elevated, and consider pitching around him with runners on base rather than challenging him in a high-leverage spot.

gamePlan.heading: Do not underestimate them based on the 1-3-1 record.
gamePlan.tip: McKinley 2 lost to Washington Wildkittens by a single run (15-14) in week 4 and tied Lincoln Lions 14-14 in week 7. Two of their four non-wins were decided by one run or a tie — this is a competitive team that can put up big numbers when it clicks.

gamePlan.heading: Shade the outfield to the gaps against Whittier and Anguera.
gamePlan.tip: Whittier's .333 ISO (2 doubles, 1 triple in 12 AB) and Anguera's triple indicate both can drive balls into the alleys. Play your outfielders slightly deeper and toward the gaps when either is batting, especially with runners on base where an extra-base hit is most costly.

gamePlan.heading: Keep Williams and Conti off base — they are your table-setter problem.
gamePlan.tip: Williams (+4 R_diff) and Conti (+3 R_diff) are the top of the order who start rallies. Williams scores 5 times for every 1 RBI, meaning the damage comes from the hitters behind him. Retire Williams and Conti quickly to face the run-producers with the bases empty, limiting the damage Dabrik, Rodriguez, and Johnston can do.
